newsitem.title: UK: Labour's 1992 graveyard holds no terrors for Blair.
newsitem.headline: Labour's 1992 graveyard holds no terrors for Blair.

text.p: Basildon has gone down in political folklore as the place which smashed former Labour Party leader Neil Kinnock's hopes of victory in Britain's last general election.

On Tuesday, the eve of the anniversary of the 1992 poll, Kinnock's successor Tony Blair and his deputy John Prescott made a triumphal visit to the town a few miles east of London to claim it as their own.

Cheering crowds shouting "Tony, Tony" were music to the ears of party workers, who are confident that at the May 1 election the town which is synonymous with working class Conservatism will at last return a Labour MP.
Some of those same workers wept openly five years ago when the news came through that David Amess had retained the seat for the Conservatives by a slim 1,480-vote majority.
Basildon was the first marginal seat to declare its result in 1992, and thus the weather vane which pointed to another five years in power for Prime Minister John Major.
"We all remember those scenes," Blair recalled at a town hall meeting. "Basildon has earned a special place in British politics."

With Labour 20 points ahead in national opinion polls, and Blair having shifted its policy to appeal to the pragmatic kind of people who live in Basildon, the party can scarcely countenance the possibility that the town will disappoint it again.
"Basildon symbolises a Britain where people want to work hard, play by the rules, own their own homes and build a better future for themselves and their family," Blair said.
"The people of Basildon particularly feel betrayed by the Conservatives -- betrayed on jobs, betrayed on tax, betrayed on basic security."
Blair stressed that Labour no longer stands for the high spending, tax raising agenda which frightened voters in Basildon away in 1992.

"The great majority of people in this country have been crying out for a serious, sensible alternative to the Conservative Party for a long time. The difference today is that they have got one," he said.

Blair and Prescott were told by one once-sceptical voter, Geraldine Evans: "I have decided to vote Labour. I truly believe that a Labour Party led by yourselves, and with the team around you, is going to produce a fairer Britain."

Amess has implicitly acknowledged that it will be a massive task for his party to hold Basildon, by jumping ship and getting himself adopted as candidate for a much safer Conservative seat a few miles away.
"The chicken's gone off to Southend," Blair said to loud laughter.
The Conservatives are making a show of defending the seat, with finance minister Kenneth Clarke paying a visit there on Monday to back the candidature of investment banker and Eurosceptic John Baron.
But there was none of the razzamatazz or the crowds that surrounded Blair.

Clarke flew in by helicopter and was rushed into a retail group's warehouse on the outskirts of the town before being whisked off to another marginal constituency. Reporters were kept out and Baron steered well away from the cameras.

Former professional boxer Terry Marsh has strapped on his gloves on behalf of the minority Liberal Democrats, but Labour is confident that its local councillor candidate Angela Smith will knock both him and Baron out of the ring.
